newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain CPI raises expectations of new BoS rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Spain CPI raises expectations of new BoS rate cut.

text.p: News on Thursday of lower-than-expected October inflation suggests to analysts that a fresh official rate cut -- which would be the seventh of the year -- may be possible before the end of December.

But the modest 0.1 percent monthly and more robust 3.5 percent yearly rise in October's Consumer Price Index (CPI) was unlikely to satisfy the Bank of Spain, which most believe will want at least one more number to confirm a steady trend.
"Now we can say that after the November data the Bank of Spain could cut the official rate before the year-end," said Elena Colomer, economist at Beta Capital.
November CPI is due on December 13.
Carmen Hernansanz, economist at Merrill Lynch, echoed: "There is a possibility the Bank of Spain will lower its key money market rate before the end of 1996."
She added that core inflation, which fell to a lower-than-expected 3.2 pct in October from 3.4 pct in September proved the underlying trend is on the downside.
"Core inflation is the most important, both for the market and for the Bank of Spain," said Juan Antonio Mielgo, economist at Bank of America in Madrid.
The low October CPI brings the economy closer to European Monetary Union (EMU), as it shortens the distance Spain has to run to comply with some of the requirements of Maastricht.
"After the Bank of Spain governor's remarks and the falling trend in Spanish CPI there are good chances of EMU convergence and new rate cuts," said an analyst who requested anonymity.
Recently the central bank governor Luis Angel Rojo said: "The economy is favourable. Spain can reasonably aspire to enter EMU from its start."

Inflation has to be lower than the average of the three most virtuous EU countries plus 150 basis points, to fulfil Maastricht's requirements. This should not prove too much of a headache for Spain, analysts said.
Spanish Budget Secretary Jose Barea said earlier this morning that Spain would fulfil three EMU requirements - inflation, the public deficit and long-term rates in 1997.
But analysts added that in order to curb price growth Spain has to work hard in the first half of 1997.
A likely turnaround in the economic cycle and a pick-up in Spanish growth could make it harder to reach the government's 1997 CPI target of 2.6 pct.

"A significative reduction in inflation should come through in the first half of 1997," said Beta's Colomer. The data should benefit from cuts in officially-regulated prices and from the declining impact of mad-cow disease on food prices, he said.
